tagline: Switchbacks climb a grade that became a gold-rush wagon road
intro: The Gold Rush Historic Byway begins with a climb from the Clearwater River: Idaho 11 rises 2,000 vertical feet in a series of switchbacks. Visit Idaho presents this scenic byway as a drive through Clearwater Valley views, rolling grain fields and forests, with Nez Perce and mining history along the way. Its published itinerary covers 42.3 miles and allows one hour and five minutes.

The original Greer grade was a Nez Perce trail. In October 1860, Elias D. Pierce and Wilbur F. Bassett discovered gold on Orofino Creek at Canal Gulch, a mile north of Pierce. During the following year's gold rush, the Walla Walla–Clearwater Road Co. built the grade's first wagon roadbed under contract with Washington Territory's legislature.

From U.S. 12 at Greer, cross the Clearwater and follow Idaho 11 up the grade toward Weippe. Weippe Prairie, south of town, is where the Lewis and Clark expedition first met the Nez Perce in September 1805. The highway turns northeast toward Pierce, passing markers for the 1885 lynching of five Chinese people, the Canal Gulch gold strike and the original Orofino. Beyond Pierce, the drive ends at Headquarters, where Idaho 11 meets Forest Roads 246 and 247.

moments.title: Weippe Prairie
moments.text: Camas grows on Weippe Prairie, where its roots historically drew Native gatherers. On September 20, 1805, Clark and the expedition's first arrivals emerged weak and starving after crossing the Bitterroots on the Lolo Trail. They encountered a large Nez Perce encampment. The Nez Perce supplied camas root cakes and other food, helped build canoes and mapped the water route west. The prairie became a National Historic Landmark in 1966 and is part of Nez Perce National Historical Park. The expedition returned in 1806 and remained with the Nez Perce from May to late June because spring came late in the Bitterroots.

moments.title: Pierce
moments.text: Pierce's wooden courthouse dates from 1862, before Idaho Territory existed. Both the building and town bear the name of Elias D. Pierce, the prospector active here in the middle of the nineteenth century. The town was Shoshone County's first seat, established while the area belonged to Washington Territory. Idaho Territory followed in 1863. Government functions continued in the courthouse until 1885. The county seat moved to Murray in 1884, then to Wallace in 1898. The courthouse is Idaho's oldest public building, and the Idaho State Historical Society operates the site.

moments.title: Headquarters
moments.text: Headquarters began as a fire protection station in 1906 and became a Potlatch company town. It was also the northeastern terminus of the Camas Prairie Railroad. Lumber-mill closures in the 1980s and 1990s eliminated many jobs and sharply affected its population. Ten miles north of Pierce, the community marks the end of Idaho 11 at its junction with Forest Roads 246 and 247.

practical: Headquarters: Portions of the byway may close in winter, and roads can be icy during winter months. (checked 2026-10-11)
